notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1436.tmp1436.opp-lat: Sermon 1, §2: the text is disturbed. '(non)' is the edition's insertion; 'sed rectius sibi soli, aut sive alius infirmus cum ipso' is garbled and is rendered for sense. 'adlucet' is corrupt; it is taken as a verb of eating such as 'accipiat', and '[eat]' is supplied. §5: 'mercedem se ... esse dixerit' is taken as 'mercedem se redditurum dixerit' (said he would give a reward). §9: corrupt. 'Aut ego et mei si negligenter' is rendered loosely, and the final clause ('quae ... docemur') appears incomplete. §12: 'charitatem contemplationis' is taken as 'caritatem vestram' (your charity). 'castitatem et charitatem' may originally have read 'castitatem et castimoniam' or similar. §13: 'nun' is read as 'non'. The closing sentence is syntactically loose.

§2: 'second epistle to the gentiles' is the text's own designation; the quotation resembles 2 Peter 1:16. 'Ambulabat Verbum' attributed to Habakkuk (cf. Hab 3:5 Vulgate). §4: 'quod draco' is odd; perhaps 'quasi draco' ('like a dragon'). §5: 'a virga serpentis edendam' is obscure, alluding to Aaron's rod-serpent (Exod 7:12). 'continentes conjuncti' read as 'continentes, conjugati'. §6: 'unitationis' read as 'imitationis'; 'hujus vocis' perhaps for 'hujus mulieris'; 'vitali donavit' read as 'vitam donavit'. Sermon III §2 is numbered 'i.' in the scan, read as 2. §3: the asterisk marks a gap before 'patientiam' (presumably 'contra iram'); the edition suggests 'subministrantur' for 'subministraverunt'; 'ante hominem' read as 'ad hominem'; 'religantur' taken as 'are bound'.

§4 'O unser' read as 'O miser'. §7 'ini. qui lues' read as 'iniqui judices' (unjust judges), uncertain; 'Bene va eas' read as 'Bene valeas'; 'dux concupiscentiae fuissent' read as 'duae concupiscentiae' (two desires); 'iactura Dei' read as 'factura Dei'. In §6 'tam magnam tran et tristiam' is corrupt; rendered as '[...] and sadness'. §8 'com upisti' read as 'concupisti'. Sermon IV §1 'origini et morti' perhaps for 'originali morti', so rendered; 'genen' read as 'generi'.

§14 'Discetur' read as 'miscetur' (is mingled). §15 paragraph number printed as '! a.'; read as 15. §10 'vim creaturam' read as 'vini creaturam'; psalm reference printed CII,4, actually Ps. 109:4 (Vulgate). §13 Apocalypse reference printed xvii,13; the verse is 17:15. §7 'a prino' read as 'a primo'. §8 'fraude multatur' rendered as 'is penalised by being cheated'; sense somewhat uncertain. §12 'Unde et sertum spineum ... imposuit': subject unexpressed, taken as the vine (i.e. the Jewish people).

nodes.text: APPENDIX XII.
SERMONS.
FIRST SERMON.—On giving up meat.

1. Dearest brothers, I ask you and I urge you that on this lawful and most sacred day, Sundays excepted, no one presume to take a midday meal, unless perhaps one whom sickness has not allowed to fast; for on other days fasting is either a remedy or a reward, but in Lent not to fast is a sin. At another time whoever fasts receives indulgence; in Lent whoever is able and does not fast will feel punishment.

2. And yet let the one who is (not) able to fast prepare for himself in his own house, more properly for himself alone, or with another sick person with him, what he is to take. And let them not invite to a meal those who are able to fast, because if they do this, not only God but also men can understand that they are not unable because of sickness, but unwilling to fast because of gluttony. Let it be enough for him that he is not able to fast. And let him rather [eat] with groaning and sighing and grief of heart, because, while others are fasting, he cannot abstain.

3. And whatever each sick person needs, let him have it prepared in private, either for himself alone or with another who is likewise close [to him], because he ought not to ask anyone healthy to a meal, lest he add to his own sin also the gluttony of another. Yet because he cannot fast, he ought to give more to the poor, so that the sins which he cannot heal by fasting he may redeem by giving alms. It is good to fast, brothers, but it is better to give alms.

4. If someone can do both, there are two goods; but if he cannot, almsgiving is better. If there is no possibility of fasting, almsgiving is sufficient without fasting; but fasting without almsgiving is not sufficient at all. Therefore if someone cannot fast, let him give alms. Almsgiving without fasting is good. If then one is able [to do] fasting with almsgiving, it is a double good; but fasting without almsgiving is no good at all, unless perhaps someone is so poor that he has nothing whatever to give. For those who have nothing from which to give, a good will is sufficient, according to what is written: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.

5. But who will there be who can excuse himself, when the Lord has said that he will give a reward even for a cup of cold water? And why did he say cold? Lest perhaps some poor man could excuse himself by a shortage of firewood, or indeed say that he did not have a pot in which to heat the water. Again, through the blessed prophet too, dearest brothers, the Lord so exhorts and urges that almsgiving be done that there is almost no poor man who can excuse himself. For he says thus: This is the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord: Break your bread for the hungry. He does not say that he should give it whole, lest perhaps that poor man should have no other; but break, he says, that is to say: even if your poverty is so great that you have only one loaf, yet break from it and give to the poor, and clothe the needy and the homeless [and bring him] into your house. If someone is so poor that he has no food, let him at least prepare a little bed for a stranger in one corner of his house.

6. What are we going to say, brothers? What excuse shall we be able to have, who, having large and spacious houses, scarcely ever deign to receive a stranger? Not knowing, or rather not believing, that in every stranger Christ is received, as he himself said: I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; and: As long as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.

7. Is it laborious and tiresome for us to receive Christ in the poor into our homeland? I fear that he may say to us: Go, and may not receive us into his blessedness. Do we despise him in the world? I fear that he may despise us in heaven, according to what he himself said: I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat; and: As long as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me; and what follows after.

8. Brothers, may God turn this away from us; for he adds this afterwards, saying: Depart from me, you cursed, go into the eternal fire. I judge no one to this sentence. Let each one attend to his own sentence; yet this I rebuke and reproach, that perhaps it sometimes happens through negligence that clothes which the poor ought to have received are spoiled by moths; and I fear that these very garments may be brought forward as testimony on the day of judgement, according to what James says: Come now, you rich, weep, howling in the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted.

9. And all the things, dearest brothers, with which, as he said, Christ threatens through his Apostle, although they terrify us greatly, yet we must not despair of God's mercy. Only if I and mine, having been negligent, wish with God's help to amend ourselves while we can, let us give more generously the alms which until now we have given more sparingly, and those things which, for past sins, with grief and groaning and hope of rest, we are taught by the Lord's mercy.

10. Therefore, as we suggested above, dearest brothers, let the richness of almsgiving commend our fasts, because fasting without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil. For just as a lamp that is lit without oil can smoke but cannot give light, so fasting without almsgiving indeed torments the flesh, but does not illuminate the soul with the light of charity. Meanwhile, at least as regards the present [season], brothers, let us so fast that we give our midday meals to the poor, so that what we would have eaten we may store not in our purses but in the bellies of the poor, because the hand of the poor is the treasury of Christ: whatever it receives, lest it perish on earth, it stores in heaven; because although what the poor man receives is consumed, yet the reward of the good work is laid up in heaven.

11. For if we take care to spend [the cost of] our midday meals on the evening meal with exquisite flavours and multiplied courses, then just as delights are not only not withdrawn from our body but even doubled, and so nothing is taken from your body, so nothing is added to the soul. This, brothers, I urge more out of fear than because I believe anything bad of you. For I know that many of you, by God's favour, both constantly receive strangers and often give to the poor. And so let what I suggest profit [them] toward this. But whoever does not do it, or perhaps was doing it rather slowly, let him make so holy and wholly pleasing a work into a habit.

12. And although I believe that, by God's inspiration, whenever feasts come round, your charity keeps chastity and charity for many days beforehand even with your own wives, yet, even if it be superfluous, I urge your charity to do what I believe you do: that through the whole of Lent and until the end of Easter you keep chastity and charity, with God's help, so that at that most holy Easter solemnity you may be clothed with the lamp of charity, whitened by alms, adorned with prayers, vigils and fasts, or with some heavenly and spiritual pearls, [at peace] not only with friends but also with enemies, so that, approaching the altar of the Lord as peacemakers with a free and secure conscience, you may receive his body and blood not to judgement but to healing.

13. But when we speak of alms, let narrow poverty not be troubled. For anyone will be able to fulfil everything when he has done what he could, because the perfect will to do is reckoned as the deed done. But he fulfils this who is willing to regard the poor man as himself, and so gives to the poor man as he would wish to be done to him if he himself were in such need; and whoever does so has fulfilled the precepts of both the New and the Old Testament, fulfilling that [word of the] Gospel: Everything whatever you wish that men should do to you, do likewise to them. For thus the law and the prophets are fulfilled unto glory, to which may the faithful Lord lead you by his protection, [according to] the law of true and perfect charity. Amen. By the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and dominion without end for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON II. — Against the Arians.

1. Come, Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, who have equal power with the Father. Come, and crush the head of the great dragon; and tell us what you are, [and] how this Arius teaches other than what you are. Speak, speak, let us hear, so that we may refute the heretics. Hear, dearest brothers, what the Lord says. I am, he says, the way, the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. According to the divinity [he is] the truth and the life, according to the humanity the way. But you, Arian heretic, who would have the life and the truth be less than divinity, it follows that you do not reach the Father. But further, Lord Jesus, crush the head of the dragon, and say what you are with the Father. Let us hear you speaking, not the heretic blaspheming; say what you are with the Father. I and the Father are one. Speak further. I am in the Father, and the Father is in me. Speak further. Whoever sees me sees the Father also.

2. Do you now believe, heretic, so great an authority? Or do you not accept his own testimony about himself, but look for other witnesses? See, those are brought in against you who will refute you. Speak, Paul, witness of God, instrument of holy mother Church, who went even to [shedding your] blood for this testimony, and laid down your life so as not to yield to false doctrine; speak. Let him hear who fears to be refuted. To each and every one you say: Have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God. Do you hear, heretic, 'equal to God'? Do you hear 'the form of God'? And you dare to call the Son less than the Father? Let another witness come too, so that in two or three witnesses the justice of the truth may be confirmed. Speak you also, holy Peter, [and say] what was revealed to you, not by flesh and blood, but by the heavenly Father: You are the Son of the living God. And in the second epistle to the gentiles: We make known to you the power and foreknowledge and greatness of our Lord Jesus Christ. Do you hear, deceiver, 'power'? Do you hear 'foreknowledge'? Do you hear 'greatness' too? In what, then, heretic, do you say Christ is less? But let a third witness also enter, so that three may speak one true testimony to the one Trinity and threefold divinity. Speak you also, holy John, who reclined upon the Saviour's breast, and saw above the heavenly wonders the Word of God. Speak, I say, what truth you perceive concerning the Son of God. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. And in the epistle: We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know what is true, and may be in his true Son; for this is the true God and eternal life.

3. But you, venomous serpent, by calling the Son less, who is true God, will not have eternal life. But to confound your obstinacy, let the Father himself bear witness to the Son, so that you seek nothing further and believe nothing further. For he says through the prophet: With you is the beginning in the day of your power. The Father is the beginning, the Son is the beginning; therefore the Father and the Son are the beginning without any beginning. With you, he says, is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendours of the saints; from the womb before the morning star I begot you. As if he were saying: So that the saints might be enlightened, you came forth from me. Nor indeed, dearly beloved, was there any other reason why even the very names, that is, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, should appear separate, except that holy men might be instructed. For the rest, what was said to Moses by the very substance of the Trinity? I am who am; and thus you shall say: He who is has sent me. Therefore the Son was begotten from the womb in the splendour of the saints. But lest you take this begetting to have been done in a fleshly or temporal way, hear how he begot him. My heart has belched forth, he says, a good Word. John the witness says: In the beginning was the Word. God the Father says: My heart has belched forth, he says, a good Word. The prophet Habakkuk says: The Word walked. You hear 'the Word', and that this was in the beginning with God, and that the Word was God. The testimony of the Trinity cries out against you through the whole world. And you, wicked Arian, bark against the whole world like a rabid dog?

4. But hear further how you may be more fully refuted, [namely] that the perfect Trinity is one true God. For the voice of the Father to the Son through the prophet is: In the splendour, he says, of the saints, from the womb I begot you. Also the voice of the same Father through the prophet about the Holy Spirit is: The Spirit, he says, went forth from me. And the voice of the Son in the Gospel, showing that the Father is in him and he in the Father, is where he says: The Father abiding in me, he does the works. The voice of the same Son also concerning the Holy Spirit, showing that as he proceeds from the Father, so also from himself, is where he says to his disciples: Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone's sins, they will be forgiven him. Hence also [the words] of the apostle Paul: If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. If, then, the Son is in the Father and from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is at once both in the Son and in the Father, the Trinity is not divided where there is perfect unity. Let the pestilent Arian depart, then, the labyrinthine one, since [he is] a dragon; let him now depart, I say, confounded and guilty, because the Trinity is one God.

5. But how could my words profit you, perverse heresy, since you are a deaf asp, stopping its ears so as not to hear the voices of the charmers? Know, however, that you are to be devoured by the rod of the serpent, when that shepherd leads back to his fold the sheep you hold captive, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd. This, then, is our shepherd, dearly beloved, who feeds and rules with a rod; he is the shepherd, he is our ruler, he the builder, he our architect. I see you, Lord Jesus, a great shepherd, feeding the sheep, seeking the stray, and, once found, carrying it back on your shoulders with joy to the flock. Indeed I see you a great architect, bearing a rod, and working many miracles with that rod. And so, brothers, I greatly fear the explanation of the rod; but when I consider the passages of the divine Scriptures, the rod is holy Mary, the rod is Christ himself, the rod is the cross. And on this, oh, what great and wondrous things he made! Ladders, by which he raised fallen man to the Father; and by these ladders, finally, holy men have ascended, the continent, the married, and the faithful, not indeed with steps of the feet, but with the steps of conduct.

6. If, then, good conduct is sought, it is found in all. For both sexes and every age have in this conduct of the saints an example for imitation. So let old men imitate the conduct of Tobit, who, though he was blind in body, showed his son the way of life in his heart; the one led him by the hand on earth, the other raised him to heaven by holy counsels. Let young men imitate holy Joseph, beautiful in body but more beautiful in mind, whom chastity had so possessed that his body could not be violated by the threats of his shameless mistress, since the Lord had already possessed his mind. Let holy virgins imitate Mary, the blessed mother of their Lord. Let widows imitate the devout widow Anna. And let married women imitate chaste Susanna; for the virgin Mary, mother of Christ, fulfilled what she knew; Anna the widow persevered in prayers and fasting to the end; chaste Susanna went to the danger of death for conjugal modesty. Now then, married women, consider what kind of imitation of this example is set before you by holy Scripture; for it does not proclaim that she was adorned outwardly with gold, necklaces or costly clothing, since she was certainly adorned within with the modesty of chastity. Indeed Christ gave life to all those for whom he established good conduct. And for this reason he himself, a man, deigned to be born of a woman, because both sexes were to be freed from death by him. We have said much, brothers. You have listened most attentively; you have eaten the Lord's feast most gladly. Repay your minister in turn, then, so that, if not by word, he may at least be fed by your prayers. The end.
SERMON III. — A Homily.

1. Brothers, we ought greatly to fear three causes through which the whole world perished: gluttony, greed, pride. For through these three causes the devil deceived Adam, the first man, saying: On whatever day you eat of this tree, at once your eyes will be opened. So let us always fear these three causes, lest, like Adam, we be damned in hell. Brothers, against gluttony let us hold to abstinence, against greed generosity, against pride humility. For this we know, that we are called Christians, that we have a guardian angel, because the Saviour himself said: Amen I say to you that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.

2. For we must believe for certain that all our works, by day as well as by night, at every hour, whether good or bad, whatever we do, are reported by that angel in the sight of God. For when the angel urges counsel on us to do good works, we believe that we always have that angel on our right; but when we think of doing evil, or attempt to commit any sins, mortal as well as small, then we have the malign devil as our instigator, so that when we think of sinning and sin, the devil rejoices and that holy angel grieves. When we speak idle and wicked words, it is the devil's counsel; but when we groan and sigh and think of doing some good works, then we have that holy angel of God as our counsellor.

3. For those three evil works which we mentioned above, that is, gluttony, greed, pride, the devil supplied to Adam through evil counsel. These three causes produce many evils, that is, sacrilege, murder, adultery, theft, avarice, lust, false witness, anger, discord, perjury. All these, through those three transgressions, have been supplied to man by the devil's craft. By these perils souls are bound in hell. So let us take up the arms of the angel of God, that is, the cross of Christ. Let us set against pride humility, against gluttony abstinence, against greed the bestowal of alms, against sacrilege true penance, against murder the love of God and neighbour, against fornication continence, against theft goodness and kindness, against avarice generosity, against lust chastity, [...] patience, against discord good concord and the truest peace, against perjury the fear of the Lord and the right way, holding a most firm faith before God and men with justice and holiness.

4. These are the angelic arms, and a strong breastplate, and a most firm shield, and the helmet of salvation. Whoever has these arms with him in every place, no devil will be able to harm him; but here and for eternity he will be safe. O dearest brothers, we ought to arm ourselves so well against the worst enemy that we may be able to overcome him, because he is ready, like a thief, to steal good works; he counsels and supplies evil things. There are many who through the boldness of the adversary are deceived by a false sense of security, and they think among themselves, saying: I am young, and I have time to enjoy the world; when I come to old age, I will do penance. O wretch, you who think this, for you do not have the space of one hour of your life, nor power over a single day.

5. Brothers, do not let this wicked security deceive you, but let us always have the day of death before our eyes, with fear and true penance. Tell me, where are the kings, where the rich, where their riches and their ornaments? They have passed away like a shadow, they have vanished like a dream; their gold and silver and all their ornaments have remained in this world, and they themselves are tormented without end in hell, where their worms do not die and their fire is not quenched. In that hell there is no voice but groaning; there is no rest there, but flame, where many seek an end in death and cannot die. For it is written: The mighty suffer torments mightily.

6. O brothers, understand, the Psalmist says: The dead will not praise you, Lord, nor all who go down into hell. Brothers, how can they name God, who are always in darkness and in a dark place, and always cry out: Woe, so dark a place, so dark a pit, so obscure a cavern, so bitter a place, so most wretched a life, so painful a dwelling! O wretches, for so short a life so long a death, for so small a comfort so long a captivity, for so small a joy so long a sorrow, for so small a gain so heavy a loss, for so small an honour such long pains, for so small a pleasure such bitter tears, such immense sighs, such mournful groans, such great [...] and sadness. There the father does not help the son, nor the son the father; there no friend is found who may redeem his friend, nor brother who may succour his brother. There penance is loved, but it is done too late. Woe! so hard a dwelling, so tormenting a flame, such immense torments.

7. There the wretched [are] with the wretched, the proud with the proud, murderers with murderers, adulterers with adulterers, unjust judges with false merchants, false monks with false maidens, false priests with false bishops, laymen likewise with the worst laymen. There the worst women [are] with the most unhappy harlots: all will be tormented in unspeakable flames, and will have no rest except on the Lord's day of the resurrection, as blessed Augustine says: On the Lord's day of the resurrection, at the hour when our Lord rose from the dead in the morning, the souls of the just come to visit their tombs and to say: Fare well, good companion, because you did well with me in this world, good vessel, dearest friend. You consented to the angelic arms rather than to the assault of the devil, for it is written: I wished to fast, to do penance, to give alms, to clothe the naked, to visit the sick, to come to church, to hear and keep the holy Scriptures, to love the servants of God; you consented to me and honoured [me], because you are the making of God, and I am the breath of life, and created by God. Rest a little while in peace, secure, and I will return to you in the eternal dwelling, so that you may see what dwelling and how great a glory God has prepared for us for ever, because happy are those who serve him, and they will shine with him like the sun, as the Lord himself says: The just will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father, and then they will rejoice with me without end. For although two desires were there, the lust of the eyes and of the mouth, you did not consent to them. Near is [the time] when you will receive with me the eternal reward, and there you will rest for ever and ever.

8. Likewise that sinful soul too, with the most wicked angel of Satan, with accusation and with its vices, speaks, saying: Alas! alas! wretched body, why did you do such evils with me? And I was with Satan with his vices, because you did not consent to the angelic arms against the snares of the devil. For you desired to eat, to drink, to live in lust, to kill, to commit adultery, to fornicate, to steal, to covet, to lie, to bear false witness, to do the works of the devil, and you did not do penance, but you failed in false security and negligence. You lie in the depths, I am tormented in hell. The day of judgement is near, when I will return to you, and you will rise on the last day, to receive the evils you worked in the world with the devil, the author of death, and you will be with me in the damnation of death, and will be tormented without end for ever and ever. O man, who hear these things, be terrified for your sins and negligences, and while you have time and space, hurry and do penance, before the door of life is shut, so that you may securely receive the rewards of glory and eternal life with the angels of God and with all the saints for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON IV. — On the Body and Blood of the Lord at Easter.

1. The greatness of the heavenly benefits exceeds the narrowness of the human mind. And therefore divine Providence has so ordained that what reason in us, overcome by the weight of the matter, could not grasp, devout faith should conceive, and robust belief should nourish understanding. Since, then, through the first transgression by Adam we were held liable to original death, the Lord, looking from on high at the point in which we were debtors as a race, restored the gift of redemption according to the nature of our captivity. That is, that for the death that was owed he should offer one not owed, because neither had we the means to live, nor he the means to die.

2. He took matter from our mortality, so that, immortality being conferred from what was his own, Life could die for the dead. And therefore, because he was about to take the body he had assumed away from our eyes and carry it to the stars, it was necessary that on this day he should consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood, so that what was once offered as the price might be honoured continually through the mystery. So that, since redemption ran daily and unwearied for the salvation of men, the offering of the redemption might also be perpetual, and that everlasting victim might live in memory, so as to be always present in grace. Truly a unique and perfect sacrifice, to be judged by faith, not by appearance, and to be assessed not by outward sight but by inward feeling.

3. Hence heavenly authority rightly confirms that the flesh of Christ is truly food, and his blood is truly drink. Let every doubt of unbelief therefore depart, since he who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness of its truth. For the invisible priest, by his word, with secret power converts visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying thus: Take and eat; for this is my body. And, repeating the sanctification: Take, he says, and drink; this is my blood (Matth. 26:26, 27). So, just as at the nod of the commanding Lord the heights of the heavens, the depths of the waves, the expanses of the lands suddenly came to be out of nothing, with equal power in the spiritual sacraments the power of the Word commands, and the effect obeys.

4. Consider, therefore, how great and how worthy of celebration are the benefits which the force of the divine blessing works. And so that it may not seem to you new and impossible that earthly and mortal things should be changed into the substance of Christ, question yourself, who have now been regenerated in Christ. Not long ago, a stranger to life, an exile from mercy, inwardly dead, you were banished from the way of salvation. Suddenly initiated into the laws of Christ and renewed by the saving mysteries, you passed into the body of the Church, not by seeing but by believing, and from a son of perdition you were found worthy to become, by a hidden purification, an adopted son of God.

5. Remaining in visible measure, you were made greater than yourself invisibly, without increase of quantity. While you were one and the same, you came to stand much higher through the advances of faith. In the outward [man] nothing was added to you, and you were wholly changed in the inner man. And thus man was made a son of Christ, and Christ was formed in the mind of man. So, just as without bodily sensation, your former baseness laid aside, you suddenly put on a new dignity, and just as you believe, not with your eyes but with your inner senses, that the Lord has healed in you what was wounded, washed away what was stained, wiped clean what was soiled: so too, when you approach the venerable altar to be refreshed with the saving food and drink, look upon the holy body and blood of your Lord with faith, marvel at it with reverence, lift up your mind, receive it with the hand of the heart, and above all take it in with an inward draught.

6. Now that manna of the law, of which it is said: He rained manna on them to eat (Ps. 77:24), tasted to each person of whatever he had longed for in his desires; what was taken was one thing, what was seen was another, and that flavour was formed invisibly in the senses of each. So that manna of the law, which fell from heaven, by the manifold sweetnesses of its nature surpassed what its merit and its kind appeared to be. And since the dispensation of the giver seasoned his creature with manifold variety, the taste supplied what the sight did not know. The novelty and worth of that food arose according to the desire of the one receiving it, and the honey-flowing gift of that rain, the manifold service of that dry shower, refreshed each person with various and different flavours.

7. This being so, what craving did there, let faith do here. So we read: Man shall come to a deep heart, and God shall be exalted (Ps. 63:7). Therefore what delight held in the throat there, let blessing work in the inner senses here. The very power of the one who consecrates gives strength to recognise and receive the sacrifice of the true body. He who then lay hidden, prefigured in the manna, let him now be made plain to you in grace. That he himself was foreshadowed in the form of that manna, the Prophet also clearly shows, saying: He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels (Ps. 77:25). And what is the bread of angels but Christ, who fills them with the food of his love and the light of his brightness? Of this bread, as the Prophet says: On the sixth day you shall gather double, but on the Sabbath you shall not gather, since in the law it is given from the first day, that is, the Lord's day, and refused on the Sabbath alone.

8. Already then it is shown that Christ was to be received by the Church, for which the resurrection consecrated the Lord's day, and it is foretold that he was to be denied by the Synagogue, to which the observance of the Sabbath belonged, since this is the seventh day, which is penalised by being cheated of the heavenly bread. Of this bread the ancient history relates: He who had gathered more did not have more, nor did he who had prepared less find less (Exod. 16:18). This body, when the priest distributes it, is as much in a small portion as it is in the whole. When the church of the faithful receives it, just as it is full in all, so it is shown to be whole in each. From this sense the apostolic saying is derived, which says: He who had much did not have too much, and he who had little did not have less (2 Cor. 8:15).

9. If we were to set bread before the hungry to eat, it would not reach each one in its entirety, because each would receive a smaller and finer part according to his share. But of this bread, when it is taken, each one has no less than all together. One receives the whole, two the whole, many the whole, without diminution, because the blessing of this sacrament knows how to be distributed and does not know how to be consumed by distribution. And so we find the form of this sacrament expressed even in the pages of the Jews. For of Melchizedek we read in Genesis: And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine, and blessed Abraham; and he was priest of God most high (Gen. 14:18, 19). In this, when the circumcision that was to come is blessed by the foreskin, that is, by the gentiles, the glory of the Church is proclaimed, and the people gained from the gentiles is set before the unbelieving synagogue.

10. This Melchizedek, then, whose genealogy or origin was hidden from the knowledge of that time, foreshadowed this sacrifice of Christ by the offering of bread and wine. Of him the Prophet declares: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109:4). For blessed Moses too, speaking of this mystery, signifies wine and blood under one name, showing the Lord's passion long beforehand in the blessing of the patriarch, saying thus: He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape (Gen. 49:11). Notice how evidently it is established that the creature of wine is to be called the blood of Christ.

11. Whatever more you may need to ask about this twofold kind, learn it from the testimony of the Lord himself. Unless, he says, you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you (John 6:54). This testimony is most evident and most powerful against the Pelagians, who, having seized on impiety, presume to assert that baptism is to be conferred on infants not for the sake of life but for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. For under these words of the Lord, by which the evangelist declares: you will not have life in you, it is plainly to be understood that every soul empty of the gift of baptism lacks not only glory but life. That this wine of the Lord's blood is to be mixed with water, the Lord showed not only by tradition but also by the very manner of his passion, since from his sacred side blood and water flowed out at the stroke of the lance. As the Prophet foretold long before, saying: He struck the rock, and waters flowed (Ps. 77:20). And the Apostle: They drank, he says, from the rock that followed them (1 Cor. 10:4). You see that whoever drinks of the grace of Christ, the mercy of Christ follows him.

12. But in Solomon too we read it foretold of Christ himself: Wisdom, he says, has built herself a house (Prov. 9:1), that is, he took on a human body, in which the fullness of the divinity dwelt. And he added: She has hewn out seven pillars. For the blessing of the Holy Spirit filled him with sevenfold grace. She has slain her victims, mixed her wine in the bowl, and prepared her table. And in what follows: Come, eat of my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you. So we read of wine mixed with water; now let us ask the reason why the Lord willed that both be mixed. When at the wedding feast of the Jews the wine, that is, faith, was failing in them, the wine, I say, was failing, because the vine refused its fruit. Of which it is said: I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns (Isa. 5:2). Hence it also placed a crown of thorns on the Redeemer's head.

13. So when the Lord, at the time of the wedding, that is, when the bridegroom who was to be joined to his Church in paschal rejoicing, turned water into wine, he clearly prefigured that the multitudes of the gentiles would live by the grace of his blood. For that peoples are signified by waters is disclosed in the sacred scriptures. So we read: These waters which you saw are peoples and nations and tongues (Apoc. 17:15). We see that in the waters a figure of the gentiles is shown, and in the wine the blood of the Lord's passion. And thus, when in the sacraments wine is mixed with water, the faithful people is incorporated and joined to Christ, and united to him by a certain bond of perfect love, so that it can say with the Apostle: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or persecution? and the rest (Rom. 8:35).

14. And God is mingled with man when sanctification has been received, when faith, and a disposition of justice, mercy and piety, is poured into his very breast. Even in the fact that we know bread to be made from numerous grains of wheat, it is established that the unity of the peoples is signified. For just as grain, which is prepared by the thorough care of one who cleans it, is brought to a white appearance by the labour of the millstones, and through water and fire is gathered into the substance of one bread, so various peoples and different nations, coming together into one faith, make of themselves one body of Christ; and the Christian people, like innumerable grains of wheat, is seen to be gathered from sacrilegious nations, with faith cleansing and sifting it, when it is separated out, and is gathered into one, as the darnel of the unbelievers passes through, and while by the instruction of the Testaments, as grain by the twofold work of the millstones, it is tended and shines, and is changed into that dignity of its first origin by native whiteness, and through the water of baptism, as through the fire of the Holy Spirit, it is made the body of that eternal bread.

15. So, just as the grains cannot be separated from the union of the bread made from them, and just as water mixed with wine can no longer return to its own substance, so all the faithful and wise, who know themselves redeemed by the blood and passion of Christ, ought to be joined to their head as inseparable members in faith, conduct and most ardent devotion, so that they cannot be parted from him by will or by necessity, nor torn away by any ambition of earthly hope, nor finally by death itself. Nor let anyone doubt that primary creatures, at the nod of power, by the presence of majesty, pass into the nature of the Lord's body, when he sees man himself made the body of Christ by the art of heavenly mercy. And just as anyone coming to the faith is still in the bond of the old debt before the words of baptism, but once these are pronounced is at once stripped of all the dregs of sin, so when the creatures to be blessed by heavenly words are placed on the sacred altars, before they are consecrated by the invocation of the highest name, the substance there is of bread and wine; but after the words of Christ, it is the body and blood of Christ.

16. What wonder is it, then, if what he could create by a word, he can by a word change once created? Indeed it would now seem to be a lesser miracle if what he is known to have made out of nothing, he is able, once made, to change into something better. Ask what can be difficult for him for whom it was easy to raise up things visible and invisible by the command of his will; for whom it was easy to fashion man from the matter of clay, and to clothe him also with the image of his divinity; for whom it is a ready thing to call him back up from the underworld, to restore him from perdition, to repair him from dust, to lift him from earth to heaven, to make an angel of a man, to render the human body conformed to the body of his glory, and to raise his creature into the fellowship of his kingdom. So that he who had taken up the body of our frailty may take us up into the body of his immortality. May he deign to prepare you by devout works for that glorious resurrection, who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
